title: Teaching
text: Theory disciplines the evidence, the evidence tests the theory, and students learn best when they work with both. In my courses, students read the research behind the textbook and then make a case of their own—taking a country’s development record, for instance, and defending a policy response before the class.

title: Teaching
text:
Courses Taught
I was the instructor of record for four undergraduate courses at George Mason University from 2021 to 2024, in person and online, designing the syllabus, assignments, and exams for each.
ECON 104: Principles of Macroeconomics Summer 2024 · Online
An introduction to thinking like an economist about the whole economy, built around a few big questions: why some nations are rich and others poor, what the Federal Reserve does, and why economies go through business cycles.
ECON 306: Intermediate Microeconomics Fall 2023 · Online
Price theory at the intermediate level: consumer choice and demand, production and costs, and how market structure shapes prices and output, practiced through weekly problem sets with an emphasis on graphical analysis.
ECON 360: Economics of Developing Areas Spring 2023, Summer 2022 · In person
Why are some countries rich and others poor? The course moves from Malthus and Solow through poverty traps, the aid debate, health and human capital, institutions, culture, state capacity, and conflict, pairing Easterly, Banerjee and Duflo, and Koyama and Rubin with research by North, Nunn, Dell, and others. Students write discussion essays and present a country case.
ECON 385: International Economic Policy Spring 2022, Fall 2021 · In person
The economic way of thinking applied to trade and international finance, including introductory microeconomics and game theory, with historical and current evidence on the consequences of trade, protectionism, and conflict. Taught for non-major students.

title: About Me
text:
I am an Economics PhD student at George Mason University. I received my bachelor’s in Economics from GMU in 2019 and my master’s in 2021. 
I am on the 2026–27 academic job market. My CV and the Research page list my current papers and drafts.
My research interests include political and applied microeconomics, historical political economy, growth, and institutional change. Of particular focus are periods of conflict and how individual behavior is shaped by those conditions. I work primarily in R, and have experience with geospatial analysis, text-as-data methods, and historical data digitization. I have taught undergraduate courses as a graduate lecturer at George Mason University, including microeconomics, macroeconomics, and international development.
I hope that my work will help build a greater understanding of the social and political questions of the past and today. Outside of academia, I enjoy reading sci-fi/fantasy, playing the latest strategy games, and traveling with my partner.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers
Late Medieval Unrest in the Holy Roman Empire: Climate, Institutions, and Documented Unrest Draft






NoneAbstract





I construct two linked datasets for the Holy Roman Empire, 1300–1520: a geolocated catalog of popular unrest and an annual panel of city-council representation, matched at city-year resolution across 306 cities. I ask whether unrest rises with wet-dry severity and whether it rises in the years institutions changed. Contrary to prior work’s positive drought association, documented unrest tends to be more frequent in wetter years, and organized actors carry the pattern. The divergence from the closest published study survives changes in estimator, functional form, and event definition; sample scope and a recording artifact remain open. Guild representation’s apparent associations with unrest come from the years in which representation changed, often as unrest’s outcome; where guilds already held seats, severe drought went with less unrest. Burgher representation shows no association but precedes guild gains. Complaints are mostly political and fiscal. Every association here is descriptive.



Did Newspaper Competition Promote Rebellion? The Case of the 1837-38 Rebellions in Quebec Draft Appendix ProMarket

with Vincent Geloso







NoneAbstract





We study the relationship between media competition and political mobilization during the Quebec Rebellion of 1837–38. Using a new spatial dataset of newspaper agents, we test whether local press competition increased rebel activity independently of newspaper ideology. We find that greater media competition strongly predicts mobilization, especially in areas where seigneurial tenure persisted, suggesting that concentrated grievances became politically activated through competitive information networks. The results remain robust after controlling for literacy and school enrollment. Overall, competitive media transformed latent discontent into active rebelliousness.



The Specter of Slavery: Newspapers During the American Civil War 






NoneAbstract





Over the course of the 19th century, the press emerged as a critical arena for shaping political narratives. This study investigates how Civil War-era newspapers strategically amplified slavery-related discourse to influence electoral outcomes in Union states between 1860 and 1864. Drawing on over one million newspaper articles, the analysis employs topic modeling and cosine similarity measures to track the salience of slavery, abolition, and racial language in the months preceding congressional elections. Slavery-related discourse intensifies in the three months prior to elections, peaking one month before. Results indicate that greater similarity to slavery-related topics is associated with significantly higher Democratic vote share, particularly in the month prior to the election. Republican vote shares show no parallel effect or a muted inverse relationship. These findings suggest that newspapers not only reflected public sentiment but acted as partisan instruments, shaping electoral behavior by modulating the salience and framing of slavery-related issues. This contributes to the literature on political communication and media partisanship by demonstrating how ideological media coverage can influence voter alignment during periods of institutional upheaval.
